newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper ends higher on moderate volumes.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper ends higher on moderate volumes.

text.p: COMEX copper futures ended higher Thursday, recovering some of Wednesday's sharp losses on moderate volumes.
Light fund and commission house buying on COMEX, and some arbitrage related activity late in the session, helped push prices back up, traders said.
"Copper was definitely overdone on the downside Wednesday and demand remains reasonable, but prices continue to swing around in two or three cent ranges," GNI New York trader Malcolm Freeman said.
COMEX September copper ended up 3.00 cents at $108.90 cents a pound, after finding some support early around 106.00 cents. Estimated final COMEX volume was 7,500 lots.
Copper prices have been recovering recently from three month lows seen in early July.

But there wasn't much momentum behind the recovery, with the LME cash-to-three month backwardation easing further to just $12.00 a tonne and the COMEX September/December spread little changed around 2.60 cents a pound.

Earlier in the day LME copper stocks rose a less-than-expected 850 tonnes Thursday to 227,800 tonnes, while COMEX copper stocks rose 233 short tons to 30,023 short tons, as the seasonally slow summer continues to ease demand.
In the past six weeks, LME warehouse stocks have increased 105,400 tonnes, taking the total to the highest level since October last year.

"During the second half of 1997, we are anticipating that global stocks of refined copper will increase to more comfortable levels, assuming no significant supply disruptions, or larger-than-expected Chinese purchases," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
"Price distribution for the nearby futures is expected to be mostly concentrated in the 95-115 cent range through year-end," he said.

Western world copper production is expected to increase by about 4.5 percent in 1997 over 1996 to 10.6 million tonnes, followed by year-over-year increases of 4.2 percent in 1988 and 3.3 pct in 1999, according to Smith Barney.
Meanwhile, year-over-year increases of 3.0 pct are expected in Western copper consumption in 1997-1999, with 1997 usage forecast at 10.9 million tonnes.
Assuming Eastern bloc net exports of 600,000 tonnes, world copper stocks could increase by 200,000 in 1997, Rinehimer said.
